Adult individuals of the black leather chiton, Katharina tunicata, can attain a maximum body length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger members of the family Mopaliidae on the Pacific coast of North America. This impressive ultimate length is not reached until after many years of slow, determinate growth, with the majority of somatic expansion occurring during the first decade of life. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability occurs at a considerably smaller size; field surveys indicate that puberty is attained at a length of 3.25 centimeters [Lp = 3.25 centimeters], a value estimated from the relative size at maturity observed in the related species Lepidochitona cinerea. This size threshold marks the point at which individuals begin to allocate resources toward gametogenesis, transitioning from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive effort. The substantial gap between the length at puberty and the ultimate length suggests a protracted period of adult life during which reproductive output can increase as the animal continues to expand its body size.

In the cold, nutrient-rich waters of the northeastern Pacific, where temperatures hover near 16 °C [T = 16 °C] for much of the active growing season, Katharina tunicata exhibits a maximum reproductive rate estimated at approximately 2,384 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,384 eggs per day]. This calculation is derived from a size-corrected extrapolation of the annual fecundity observed in the smaller chiton Lepidochitona cinerea, adjusted for the substantially larger body volume of K. tunicata. The daily output underscores the species high fecundity, which is characteristic of many broadcast-spawning marine invertebrates that rely on external fertilisation and face high rates of larval mortality. Reproductive output at this level is likely sustained only during the peak of the spawning season, when energetic reserves are at their maximum and environmental conditions are most favorable for gamete release and subsequent larval development. Under these thermal conditions, the species can produce a prodigious number of offspring, though the actual recruitment to the benthic population is typically far lower due to the vicissitudes of planktonic life.

At the moment of syngamy, the newly fertilised ovum of Katharina tunicata has a wet weight of just 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], a minuscule mass that reflects the lecithotrophic nature of the early embryo. This value is based on the typical egg diameter range of 160 to 200 micrometers reported for the related chiton Lepidochitona cinerea, from which the volume and thus the wet weight were calculated assuming a spherical shape and a density near unity. Because the egg contains a finite yolk supply, the developing larva must undergo a rapid trophic switch before the endogenous reserves are exhausted. Remarkably, settlement and metamorphosis follow only a few hours after hatching, meaning that the wet weight of the post-metamorphic juvenile is only marginally larger than that of the fertilised egg. Field-collected recruits have a measured wet weight at metamorphosis of 0.0000043 grams , indicating that nearly the entire yolk volume is conserved through the brief larval phase and that very little somatic growth occurs during the free-swimming period. This near-isometric transition from embryo to benthic juvenile is an adaptation that minimizes the energetic cost of planktonic existence.

Despite their microscopic beginnings, juvenile black leather chitons gradually increase in mass and length as they graze the biofilm of diatoms and algae covering the rocky intertidal substrate. The protracted growth trajectory of Katharina tunicata is reflected in its maximum recorded life span, which, under the stable thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], is estimated at approximately 6,205 days [am = approximately 6,205 days]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 17 years, is notably long for a polyplacophoran mollusk and likely exceeds the values reported for many smaller chiton species that exhibit faster growth and earlier reproductive senescence. The life span estimate is thought to be conservative, as growth mark analyses on older individuals have revealed shell annuli consistent with a minimum of 12 years, suggesting that the actual maximum may be considerably greater. Such extended longevity allows for repeated annual spawning events and the accumulation of substantial lifetime reproductive output. In the absence of significant predation from sea stars or fish, adult mortality is largely attributable to physical disturbance from wave action and the gradual senescence of physiological systems, culminating in natural death after the completion of the life cycle.

The life history strategy of Katharina tunicata thus combines a remarkably small initial body mass with a large adult size, spanning several orders of magnitude in wet weight from the fertilised ovum at 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams] to the asymptotic adult length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters]. This dramatic size range is accompanied by a relatively early attainment of reproductive maturity at 3.25 centimeters [Lp = 3.25 centimeters], after which individuals continue to grow and accumulate reproductive potential over a lifespan that may exceed 6,205 days [am = 6,205 days] at 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The consistency of these measurements with patterns observed in other mopaliid chitons underscores the role of slow growth, delayed senescence, and high fecundity in the evolutionary success of this intertidal herbivore along the wave-exposed shores of the northeastern Pacific.
